Behind the numbers

Google Analytics

Every campaign I run is tracked back to Google Analytics, because opinions about what's working are only useful until the data disagrees with them. I look at sessions, users, and goal conversion rate broken down by device — desktop, mobile and tablet all behave differently, and treating them the same is one of the quickest ways to waste ad spend.

The report above is the kind of view I pull for clients every month: where the traffic is actually coming from, which device category converts best, and where drop-off is happening in the funnel. It's not about collecting numbers for a slide — it's about deciding what to fix next.

Where every project starts

SEO Audits

Before I touch a single keyword or page, I run a full SEO audit — technical health, backlink profile, site traffic, error identification, and where the site currently ranks. It's the diagnostic step that tells me whether a site's problem is content, structure, speed, or authority, instead of guessing and fixing the wrong thing first.

A good audit also sets the baseline. Without knowing exactly where a site stood on day one, it's impossible to prove what the work afterward actually changed — and proving impact is half of what keeps a client around.

Fixing what search engines see

Google Search Console

Search Console is where I check how a site is actually performing in Google's eyes — total clicks, impressions, average CTR and average position, tracked over weeks so I can see whether a change actually moved the needle. It's also where indexing errors, coverage issues, and manual actions show up first, long before they'd show up as a traffic drop in Analytics.

On one project, using this data to identify and resolve a handful of key SEO issues was enough to steadily lift impressions over a couple of months — small technical fixes, tracked properly, add up.
